pharm: A synthetic form of vitamin B12 that is converted to the active coenzymes methylcobalamin and adenosylcobalamin, essential for DNA synthesis, red cell formation and neurological function
quick: Deficiency: IM 100-1000 mcg daily to weekly then monthly maintenance; oral 1000-2000 mcg daily; nasal 500 mcg weekly
Oral tablets can be taken with or without food; take consistently
Recommended to maintain adequate B12; required amounts are safe in pregnancy
Recommended amounts are safe and support infant B12 needs
No specific adjustment; standard supplementation used
Chronic alcohol use may impair B12 absorption; no direct interaction
Serum B12, full blood count/reticulocytes, serum potassium during initial correction
summary: Cyanocobalamin is a synthetic form of vitamin B12 used to treat and prevent vitamin B12 deficiency, including pernicious anaemia, deficiency from malabsorption or dietary lack, and to meet increased requirements. In the body it is converted to the active coenzymes methylcobalamin and adenosylcobalamin, which are required for DNA synthesis, normal haematopoiesis and myelin maintenance. Deficiency from malabsorption (e.g. pernicious anaemia, gastrectomy, ileal disease) is usually treated parenterally (intramuscular injection), as intrinsic-factor-dependent oral absorption is impaired; dietary deficiency can be managed with oral or parenteral B12. High-dose oral therapy and intranasal forms are also used for maintenance. During initial correction of severe deficiency, brisk new red-cell production can cause hypokalaemia, so potassium should be monitored. It is generally very well tolerated.
indications: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency, including pernicious anaemia and deficiency due to malabsorption (gastrectomy, ileal resection, intestinal disease) or inadequate dietary intake
Prevention/treatment of increased B12 requirements (e.g. some haemolytic, hepatic, renal or malignant conditions, and dietary insufficiency in vegans)
Schilling test reagent (diagnostic) and other clinical uses per local labelling

dosage.d: IM (or deep SC) 100-1000 mcg; common schedules give daily/alternate-day doses initially, then 100-1000 mcg every 1-3 months for maintenance
dosage.n: Parenteral route preferred when absorption is impaired
High oral doses are absorbed by passive diffusion independent of intrinsic factor

dosage.d: 500 mcg in one nostril once weekly (per product labelling)
dosage.n: Use only after haematologic remission with parenteral therapy

dosage.d: Periodic IM 100-1000 mcg monthly, or daily oral high-dose B12
dosage.n: Lifelong therapy needed in pernicious anaemia / permanent malabsorption

admin: Give parenteral cyanocobalamin by intramuscular or deep subcutaneous injection; the intravenous route is generally not recommended
Take oral tablets consistently; high oral doses can be effective even when intrinsic factor is lacking, via passive diffusion
For intranasal products, follow the device instructions and avoid use during nasal congestion that may impair absorption
Confirm the diagnosis and obtain baseline blood counts and B12/folate before treatment where possible
Monitor serum potassium during the initial response in severe megaloblastic anaemia
Continue maintenance therapy lifelong in pernicious anaemia and other permanent causes of malabsorption
moa: Cyanocobalamin is converted in the body to the active cobalamin coenzymes methylcobalamin and 5-deoxyadenosylcobalamin. Methylcobalamin is a cofactor for methionine synthase, which converts homocysteine to methionine and regenerates tetrahydrofolate needed for DNA (thymidylate) synthesis; deficiency impairs DNA synthesis and causes megaloblastic anaemia. Adenosylcobalamin is a cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase in fatty-acid and amino-acid metabolism; deficiency leads to accumulation of methylmalonic acid and abnormal myelin, producing the neurological features of B12 deficiency. Replacing B12 restores these pathways, correcting anaemia and stabilising or improving neurological function.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to cyanocobalamin, cobalt or any component
Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy / tobacco amblyopia (cyanocobalamin may worsen optic atrophy - use hydroxocobalamin instead)
relative: Suspected folate deficiency (treating B12 alone can mask folate deficiency and worsen neuropathy if B12 is actually deficient - assess both)
Severe megaloblastic anaemia (risk of hypokalaemia and, rarely, thrombocytosis during early treatment)
monitor: Serum B12 and folate; full blood count and reticulocyte response
Serum potassium during initial correction of severe anaemia
Neurological status in patients with neuropathy
Haematocrit in patients with polycythaemic tendency

preg: Vitamin B12 is required during pregnancy, and recommended dietary/replacement amounts are considered safe. Deficiency should be corrected, as adequate maternal B12 is important for fetal neurological development.
lact: Vitamin B12 is present in breast milk and is needed by the infant. Recommended supplemental amounts are safe during breastfeeding and help maintain adequate infant B12, particularly in vegan or deficient mothers.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is required in renal impairment. Standard B12 supplementation is used; B12 status may be altered in chronic kidney disease and should be assessed clinically.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is required in hepatic impairment.

major: Chloramphenicol - may blunt the haematologic response to B12 in anaemia
moderate: Metformin - long-term use can reduce B12 absorption and lower B12 levels
Proton pump inhibitors and H2-receptor antagonists - reduce B12 absorption from food/oral sources with prolonged use
Colchicine and aminosalicylates - may impair B12 absorption
minor: Excess alcohol or potassium-losing states may affect B12 status and the early treatment response
interactions.food: Dietary B12 from animal products; oral tablets can be taken with or without food
interactions.alcohol: Chronic heavy alcohol use can impair B12 absorption and contribute to deficiency
interactions.diagnostics: Treatment raises serum B12; can mask folate deficiency on testing - measure both before treatment; large doses may interfere with some folate assays

common: Injection-site pain or reaction (with IM administration)
serious: Hypokalaemia during initial correction of severe megaloblastic anaemia
Pulmonary oedema and congestive heart failure early in treatment of severe anaemia (rare)
rare: Thrombosis/peripheral vascular thrombosis during early treatment of severe deficiency
emergency: Severe hypokalaemia with arrhythmia during early high-intensity treatment

monitoring: Serum B12 (and folate) to confirm deficiency and response
Full blood count and reticulocyte count to confirm haematologic recovery
Serum potassium during the first days of treating severe megaloblastic anaemia
Neurological assessment in patients presenting with neuropathy
Haematocrit in patients with a polycythaemic tendency
counsel: This is vitamin B12, used to treat or prevent a deficiency that can cause anaemia and nerve problems
If you have pernicious anaemia or absorption problems, you will usually need lifelong injections or high-dose tablets - do not stop without advice
Take oral doses at the same time each day; injections are given by a nurse or as instructed
Tell your doctor if you also lack folate, as both may need treating
Report rash, itching or breathing difficulty after a dose (allergic reaction)
Keep up with blood tests so your treatment can be adjusted
pk: Haematologic response begins within days (reticulocytosis within 3-5 days)
IM peak plasma levels within about 1 hour; oral absorption is partly intrinsic-factor dependent
Body stores are large (mainly hepatic) and turnover is slow; deficiency develops over months to years if intake stops
Single IM doses replete stores for weeks to months; maintenance typically monthly or daily oral
Store at room temperature, protected from light; do not freeze injectable solution
pearls: Pernicious anaemia and other malabsorptive causes usually need parenteral B12; high-dose oral B12 can work via passive (intrinsic-factor-independent) diffusion
Watch for hypokalaemia in the first days of treating severe megaloblastic anaemia (brisk erythropoiesis consumes potassium)
Assess and treat folate too - giving B12 alone can mask folate deficiency, and giving folate alone can mask B12 deficiency while neuropathy progresses
Avoid cyanocobalamin in Leber's optic neuropathy/tobacco amblyopia - use hydroxocobalamin
Long-term metformin or PPI use can cause/worsen B12 deficiency
missed: If you take oral B12 and miss a dose, take it when you remember; if it is nearly time for the next dose, skip it - do not double up. If you miss a scheduled injection, arrange to receive it as soon as possible, as missing maintenance doses in pernicious anaemia can let deficiency return.
overdose: Vitamin B12 has very low toxicity; excess is largely excreted in the urine, and overdose is not associated with significant harm. No specific treatment is usually required beyond supportive care.
